description_en: A water reservoir topped by astūpaand built in ŚS 1276 (1354 CE).The monument is found 500 meters south-east of Dull, on the side of the main path to the mediieval capital of the Khaśa Malla empire (12th-14th century).The monument is built in large blocks of hewn stone. In contains a single, rectangular room to which access is made from a door to the north-east. Three small niches are carved on the inside walls. At the centre of the room are receeding steps allowing the creation of a pool of clear water. Above the flat roof of the water tank is a central stūpa (DLK0160-001). It is comparable to the stūpa engraved on the south side of the Kīrtikhambā stone memorial pillar (DLK0260-001), which was installed in ŚS 1279 (1357 CE).The lintel of the door is of special importance as it contains the dated inscription of the reservoir's donor. The inscription indicates that it was built in ŚS 1276 (1354 CE) by Deva Varmā (Andolfatto 2019, p. 96;Pant 2009, 301). Deva Varmā was a ministre of king Pṛthvīmalla (r. 1338-1358). He is known for building another reservoir, also topped by a stūpa, in Kuchi (Achham district). The text of the inscription also mentions that the reservoir is ornamented with five stūpa ("caityapaṃcakasaṃyuktā"). This would indicate that four stūpa are now missing. They were probably placed in a quincunx plan. Their dismantling (if they were ever built) must have happened before the 1950's as the picture of the monument taken in 1954 by Giuseppe Tucci already shows a single stūpa (Tucci 1956, fig. 54).This a unique monument in the Himalayas.
monument_assessment: Slightly damaged (minor damages such as minor cracks, plants, missing stones in plinths), Surface damages, Restored

historical_events.event_description: The year of construction of the reservoir is known from the inscription engraved on the door lintel. As for most inscriptions of the time, the main body of text is written in a Nāgarī script, preceeded by the mantra of Avalokiteśvara (oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ) written in the Rañjana script. The same is observed on the two-sided inscription of the Kīrtikhambā (DLK0260-001).The text of the inscription, published by Giuseppe Tucci (1956, p. 45), is as follow:Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ(Rañjana script)1.oṃ svasti śrīśāke 1276 pauṣe vadi 2 śukravāśare mahārājādhirājaparameśvaraparamabhaṭṭārakaparamadhārmi[ka]2.paramakalpadrumāvatāraśrīmatpṛthvīmalladevavijayarājye|mahāmatyaśrīyaśovarmadevānāṃ samaye||3.naṣṭā śrīr bhi(sic)marājasya dhararājasya dhīmataḥ|cchatyālavaṃśatilakaḥ sūnur graṃthadvavarmaṇaḥ||nāvalladevyā saṃjāto||4.devavarmā mahāmatiḥ|tenāpūrvatarā vāpī nirmitā amaravallabhā||caityapaṃcakasaṃyuktā vasati[r]buddhasaṃtateḥ|vi5.śrāmabhūmi śrāntānāṃ jīvitaṃ sarvadehināṃ mahāmatya śrīmaddevavarmadevaiḥ sarvasattvopakārārthaṃ svakīyokta6.budhyā(sic)nūtanarītyā | devānām api vallabhā | vāpī viracitā likhita dharmadāsena | iti subham astuThe translation published by Mahes Raj Pant (2009, p. 301-302), goes as follows:śrīśāke 1276 pauṣe vadi 2 śukravāśare mahārājādhirājaparameśvaraparamabhaṭṭārakaparamadhārmikaparamakalpadrumāvatāraśrīmatpṛthvīmalladevavijayarājye |mahāmatyaśrīmatyaśovarmadevānāṃ samaye ||naptā śrīr bhimarājasya dhararājasya dhīmataḥ |chatyālavaṃśatilakaḥ sūnur graṃthadvavarmaṇaḥ ||nāvalladevyāḥ saṃjāto || devavarmā mahāmatiḥ |tenāpūrvatarā vāpī nirmitā amaravallabhā ||caityapaṃcakasaṃyuktā vasati buddhasaṃtateḥ |viśrāmabhūmi śrāntānāṃ jīvitaṃ sarvadehināṃ mahāmatyaśrīmaddevavarmadevaiḥ sarvasattvopakārārātha svakīyāktabudhyā nūtanarītyā | devānām api vallabhā | vāpī viracitā ||Translation:In the glorious [year of] Sake 1276, in Pauṣa, in the waning moon, on the 2nd, on Friday; in the realm of victory of the illustrious Pṛthvīmalladeva, who is the supreme king of great kings, the supreme lord, the supreme king and a supremely pious [man] (paramadhārmika), the supreme incarnation of the Wishing Tree; during the time of the great minister (mahāmātya) the illustriousYasovarmadeva-he who is the great-minded (mahāmati) Devavarmā, the ornament (tilaka) of the Chatyāla family, the grandson of glorious Bhīmarāja [and] the wise Dhanarāja, the son of the Varmā named Grantha, and born of Navalladevī, built an unprecedented water reservoir (vāpī) which is dear to the gods, is endowed with fivecaitya-s and is a residence for the progeny of the Buddha, a place (bhumī) to rest for those who are weary, and life to all living creatures. •The Great Minister the illustrious Devavarmadeva built a water reservoir, dear even to the gods, for the benefit of all beings in accordance with his own intention, as stated [above], using a new method.
